text: AI/ML Software Engineer Roadmap A practical 4–5 month plan for a B.Tech student with classes + GATE preparation and only 1–2 hours/day. Is 1–2 Hours Daily Enough? Yes. With your current constraints, 1–2 focused hours every day is enough to make meaningful progress in 4–5 months. The goal should not be to master every AI/ML topic. The goal is to build a strong, employable foundation and 2–3 production-quality projects while keeping GATE as a major priority. Recommended split: 60–90 minutes on normal class days, 90–120 minutes when you have more time. Use weekends for longer project sessions if possible. Month 1 — Software Engineering Foundation Goal: Become comfortable writing clean Python programs and solving interview-style problems. Python Functions, OOP, exceptions, modules, virtual environments, APIs, logging, testing basics. DSA Arrays, strings, hashing, two pointers, sliding window, stack, queue, linked list, binary search. Month 2 — Machine Learning Learn: train/validation/test split, preprocessing, regression, logistic regression, decision trees, random forest, gradient boosting/XGBoost, clustering, PCA, cross-validation, precision/recall/F1, ROC-AUC, overfitting, regularization, feature engineering. Month 3 — Deep Learning + GenAI Foundations • PyTorch fundamentals and tensors. • Neural networks, loss functions, optimizers and backpropagation. • CNN and transfer learning basics. • Transformer architecture at a conceptual level. • Tokens, embeddings, context windows and LLM basics. • Hugging Face basics. Important: Do not get stuck implementing every neural-network algorithm from scratch. Understand the concepts and learn how to use them in real applications. Month 4 — LLM Engineering + Backend • Prompt engineering and structured outputs. • Embeddings and semantic search. • RAG architecture. • Vector databases: learn one deeply (FAISS, Qdrant, Chroma, or pgvector). • Tool/function calling. • FastAPI + PostgreSQL. • Docker basics. • Authentication, validation, error handling and API design.

Month 5 — Production + Job Preparation • Deploy at least 1–2 projects. • Learn cloud fundamentals on one platform: AWS, GCP or Azure. • Learn MLflow and basic model monitoring. • Learn basic AI system design. • Revise DSA continuously. • Prepare ML, GenAI and project interview questions. • Polish GitHub, resume and LinkedIn. • Start applying for internships and entry-level roles.

Research Note — LLD Practice Platform 1. Problem Understanding Low-Level Design (LLD) is an important software engineering skill used in technical interviews and real-world application development. However, learners often struggle to practice LLD effectively because understanding design principles from theory is different from actually designing a system. A learner may understand concepts such as: Classes and objects Encapsulation Inheritance Composition Interfaces SOLID principles Design patterns but still have difficulty applying them to a real problem such as a Parking Lot, Elevator System, or Vending Machine. A major challenge is also getting useful feedback. In traditional practice, learners may write a design and compare it with articles, videos, or reference solutions. This does not always explain: What was good about their design Which responsibilities were incorrectly assigned Whether the design is extensible Whether the chosen relationships make sense What trade-offs were missed How the design could be improved This creates an opportunity for a focused LLD practice platform that allows learners to solve problems and receive structured, explainable feedback. 2. Existing Ap

ould be improved This creates an opportunity for a focused LLD practice platform that allows learners to solve problems and receive structured, explainable feedback. 2. Existing Approaches and Tools Researched Several existing approaches can help learners practice software design. Coding Practice Platforms Platforms such as LeetCode and HackerRank primarily focus on algorithmic and coding problems.

Their strengths include: Large problem collections Structured practice Submission workflows Immediate feedback for executable solutions However, traditional coding platforms are generally optimized for problems where correctness can be automatically determined through test cases. LLD is different because there can be multiple valid designs for the same problem. For example, two learners may use different class structures or design patterns for an Elevator System and both may produce reasonable solutions. Online LLD Resources and Tutorials Many websites, blogs, courses, and videos provide LLD questions and reference implementations. These resources are useful for: Learning design patterns Understanding common system designs Studying example implementations Preparing for interviews However, they are generally content-oriented rather than practice-oriented. A learner usually has to: Read a problem. Create a solution independently. Compare it manually with a reference solution. Decide what could be improved. This process provides limited personalized feedback. AI Coding Assistants Modern LLM-based tools can analyze code and provide explanations or suggestions. They are useful because t

This process provides limited personalized feedback. AI Coding Assistants Modern LLM-based tools can analyze code and provide explanations or suggestions. They are useful because they can evaluate qualitative aspects that are difficult to express through simple automated test cases. For LLD, an LLM can potentially reason about: Responsibilities Separation of concerns Design patterns

Extensibility Relationships Trade-offs However, relying entirely on an LLM introduces problems such as: Subjective evaluation Inconsistent responses Hallucinations Dependence on an external API Difficulty guaranteeing deterministic scoring Therefore, using an LLM alone is not ideal for a reliable practice platform. 3. Key Gaps Identified The research suggests several gaps in existing approaches. Gap 1 — Limited LLD-Specific Practice Most coding practice platforms focus on algorithms and executable code rather than object- oriented design reasoning. Gap 2 — Limited Personalized Feedback Reference solutions show learners what an answer could look like, but they do not necessarily explain the strengths and weaknesses of the learner's own design. Gap 3 — Difficulty Automating Subjective Evaluation LLD cannot always be evaluated using simple unit tests because multiple designs may be correct. Gap 4 — Lack of Explainable Evaluation A score by itself is not particularly useful for learning. Learners need to understand why a design received that score and what they should improve. Gap 5 — LLM Reliability Although LLMs are useful for qualitative feedback, using them as the only evaluator in

rstand why a design received that score and what they should improve. Gap 5 — LLM Reliability Although LLMs are useful for qualitative feedback, using them as the only evaluator introduces reliability and consistency concerns. 4. Proposed Product Direction The proposed solution is a lightweight LLD Practice Platform focused specifically on design practice and feedback.

The learner workflow is: Select Problem → Start Attempt → Write Solution → Save Draft → Submit → Evaluate → Receive Feedback → Review History The platform contains a small set of LLD problems such as: Parking Lot Elevator System Vending Machine Movie Ticket Booking Each problem contains requirements and evaluation criteria. The learner submits a design solution as text. The platform then evaluates it using two complementary approaches. Deterministic Evaluation A rule-based evaluator checks predictable design indicators such as: Classes Responsibilities States Relationships Design patterns Trade-offs This provides a consistent baseline. AI Evaluation Google Gemini evaluates qualitative aspects such as: Design quality Separation of concerns Extensibility Trade-offs Strengths Improvements The two results are combined into a hybrid score. The MVP uses: 40% Deterministic Evaluation + 60% AI Evaluation If the AI service fails, the deterministic evaluator acts as a fallback so that the learner can still receive useful feedback.

5. Product and Architecture Direction The MVP intentionally uses a simple architecture: React → Express → MongoDB The frontend provides the learner experience, while the Express backend manages problems, attempts, and evaluation. MongoDB stores problem and attempt data. The evaluation layer is separated from the API layer so that additional evaluators can be introduced later. A future version could support additional evaluation methods such as: Code analysis UML/diagram evaluation Reference design comparison Expert-reviewed rubrics More advanced static analysis For larger-scale usage, AI evaluation could also be moved to asynchronous background workers using a queue system such as Redis or Kafka. These additions are intentionally outside the MVP because the primary objective is to demonstrate the core learning workflow and evaluation model within a limited implementation period. 6. Conclusion The research indicates that existing coding platforms are strong at evaluating executable solutions, while LLD learning requires more qualitative feedback around design decisions and trade-offs. The proposed LLD Practice Platform addresses this gap by combining: LLD-specific problems Attempt-b

rning requires more qualitative feedback around design decisions and trade-offs. The proposed LLD Practice Platform addresses this gap by combining: LLD-specific problems Attempt-based practice Explainable feedback Deterministic checks LLM-based qualitative evaluation Hybrid scoring AI failure fallback Attempt history

The result is a focused practice environment that helps learners move beyond simply reading reference designs toward actively designing systems and understanding how their design decisions can be improved.

Which of the following provides independence between application and data storage? A) Logical data independence B) Physical data independence C) View level D) Internal schema ✅ Answer: B 4. Data Abstraction helps in: A) Removing constraints B) Hiding irrelevant details C) Increasing data redundancy D) None of the above ✅ Answer: B 5. A) CREATE B) INSERT C) UPDATE D) SELECT ✅ Answer: A

Research Note — LLD Practice Platform 1. Problem Understanding Low-Level Design (LLD) is an important software engineering skill used in technical interviews and real-world application development. However, learners often struggle to practice LLD effectively because understanding design principles from theory is different from actually designing a system. A learner may understand concepts such as: Classes and objects Encapsulation Inheritance Composition Interfaces SOLID principles Design patterns but still have difficulty applying them to a real problem such as a Parking Lot, Elevator System, or Vending Machine. A major challenge is also getting useful feedback. In traditional practice, learners may write a design and compare it with articles, videos, or reference solutions. This does not always explain: What was good about their design Which responsibilities were incorrectly assigned Whether the design is extensible Whether the chosen relationships make sense What trade-offs were missed How the design could be improved This creates an opportunity for a focused LLD practice platform that allows learners to solve problems and receive structured, explainable feedback. 2. ould be improved This creates an opportunity for a focused LLD practice platform that allows learners to solve problems and receive structured, explainable feedback. 2. Existing Approaches and Tools Researched Several existing approaches can help learners practice software design. Coding Practice Platforms Platforms such as LeetCode and HackerRank primarily focus on algorithmic and coding problems.

Their strengths include: Large problem collections Structured practice Submission workflows Immediate feedback for executable solutions However, traditional coding platforms are generally optimized for problems where correctness can be automatically determined through test cases. LLD is different because there can be multiple valid designs for the same problem. For example, two learners may use different class structures or design patterns for an Elevator System and both may produce reasonable solutions. Online LLD Resources and Tutorials Many websites, blogs, courses, and videos provide LLD questions and reference implementations. These resources are useful for: Learning design patterns Understanding common system designs Studying example implementations Preparing for interviews However, they are generally content-oriented rather than practice-oriented. A learner usually has to: Read a problem. Create a solution independently. Compare it manually with a reference solution. Decide what could be improved. This process provides limited personalized feedback. AI Coding Assistants Modern LLM-based tools can analyze code and provide explanations or suggestions. They are useful because t

This process provides limited personalized feedback. AI Coding Assistants Modern LLM-based tools can analyze code and provide explanations or suggestions. They are useful because they can evaluate qualitative aspects that are difficult to express through simple automated test cases. For LLD, an LLM can potentially reason about: Responsibilities Separation of concerns Design patterns

Extensibility Relationships Trade-offs However, relying entirely on an LLM introduces problems such as: Subjective evaluation Inconsistent responses Hallucinations Dependence on an external API Difficulty guaranteeing deterministic scoring Therefore, using an LLM alone is not ideal for a reliable practice platform. 3. Key Gaps Identified The research suggests several gaps in existing approaches. Gap 1 — Limited LLD-Specific Practice Most coding practice platforms focus on algorithms and executable code rather than object- oriented design reasoning. Gap 2 — Limited Personalized Feedback Reference solutions show learners what an answer could look like, but they do not necessarily explain the strengths and weaknesses of the learner's own design. Gap 3 — Difficulty Automating Subjective Evaluation LLD cannot always be evaluated using simple unit tests because multiple designs may be correct. Gap 4 — Lack of Explainable Evaluation A score by itself is not particularly useful for learning. Learners need to understand why a design received that score and what they should improve. Gap 5 — LLM Reliability Although LLMs are useful for qualitative feedback, using them as the only evaluator in

rstand why a design received that score and what they should improve. Gap 5 — LLM Reliability Although LLMs are useful for qualitative feedback, using them as the only evaluator introduces reliability and consistency concerns. 4. Proposed Product Direction The proposed solution is a lightweight LLD Practice Platform focused specifically on design practice and feedback.

The learner workflow is: Select Problem → Start Attempt → Write Solution → Save Draft → Submit → Evaluate → Receive Feedback → Review History The platform contains a small set of LLD problems such as: Parking Lot Elevator System Vending Machine Movie Ticket Booking Each problem contains requirements and evaluation criteria. The learner submits a design solution as text. The platform then evaluates it using two complementary approaches. Deterministic Evaluation A rule-based evaluator checks predictable design indicators such as: Classes Responsibilities States Relationships Design patterns Trade-offs This provides a consistent baseline. AI Evaluation Google Gemini evaluates qualitative aspects such as: Design quality Separation of concerns Extensibility Trade-offs Strengths Improvements The two results are combined into a hybrid score. The MVP uses: 40% Deterministic Evaluation + 60% AI Evaluation If the AI service fails, the deterministic evaluator acts as a fallback so that the learner can still receive useful feedback.

5. Product and Architecture Direction The MVP intentionally uses a simple architecture: React → Express → MongoDB The frontend provides the learner experience, while the Express backend manages problems, attempts, and evaluation. MongoDB stores problem and attempt data. The evaluation layer is separated from the API layer so that additional evaluators can be introduced later. A future version could support additional evaluation methods such as: Code analysis UML/diagram evaluation Reference design comparison Expert-reviewed rubrics More advanced static analysis For larger-scale usage, AI evaluation could also be moved to asynchronous background workers using a queue system such as Redis or Kafka. These additions are intentionally outside the MVP because the primary objective is to demonstrate the core learning workflow and evaluation model within a limited implementation period. 6. Conclusion The research indicates that existing coding platforms are strong at evaluating executable solutions, while LLD learning requires more qualitative feedback around design decisions and trade-offs. The proposed LLD Practice Platform addresses this gap by combining: LLD-specific problems Attempt-b

rning requires more qualitative feedback around design decisions and trade-offs. The proposed LLD Practice Platform addresses this gap by combining: LLD-specific problems Attempt-based practice Explainable feedback Deterministic checks LLM-based qualitative evaluation Hybrid scoring AI failure fallback Attempt history

The result is a focused practice environment that helps learners move beyond simply reading reference designs toward actively designing systems and understanding how their design decisions can be improved.

Answer: • DBMS (Database Management System) is software used to store, manage, and retrieve data. It does not necessarily support relationships between data. • RDBMS (Relational Database Management System) is a type of DBMS that stores data in related tables and maintains relationships using Primary Keys and Foreign Keys. Or DBMS is software used to manage data, whereas RDBMS is an advanced type of DBMS that stores data in related tables and uses primary and foreign keys to maintain relationships while ensuring data integrity through ACID properties. By: Deepak Sikhwal -Mur2301241 Q3. What are ACID Properties in DBMS? Answer: ACID properties are four properties of database transactions that ensure data remains accurate, consistent, and reliable. ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and

r: ACID properties are four properties of database transactions that ensure data remains accurate, consistent, and reliable. ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability. • Atomicity: A transaction is completed entirely or not at all. If one step fails, the whole transaction is rolled back. • Consistency: A transaction keeps the database in a valid state and follows all rules and constraints. • Isolation: Multiple transactions can run simultaneously without interfering with each other. • Durability: Once a transaction is committed, the changes are permanently saved, even if the system crashes. By: Deepak Sikhwal -Mur2301241 Q4. What is the difference between a Primary Key and a Unique Constraint? Answer: • A Primary Key uniquely identifies each record in a table. It cannot contain NULL values or duplicate values.

• A Unique Constraint also ensures that values are unique, but it can contain NULL values (in most RDBMSs), and a table can have multiple unique constraints. By: Deepak Sikhwal -Mur2301241 Q5. What is a view in SQL? Answer: A view is a virtual table created from a SELECT query that displays data from one or more tables without storing it, helping simplify queries and improve security. The Inverse Fourier Transform is a mathematical operation that converts a function from its frequency-domain representation back to the time domain. If a signal has been transformed into the frequency domain using the Fourier Transform, the Inverse Fourier Transform is used to retrieve the original time-domain signal. The Inverse Fourier Transform formula is mathematically expressed as: x(t)= 1 2π -∞ ∞ X(ω) e jωt dω Where: x(t) represents the time-domain signal. X(ω) is the Fourier transform of the signal, representing its frequency-domain equivalent. ω is the angular frequency. j is the imaginary unit. I n essence, the Inverse Fourier Transform takes a frequency spectrum, X(ω), and reconstructs the original signal x(t)x(t)x(t) in the time domain. The formula ensures that no information is lost during the transformation from time to frequency and back. We can derive it by taking the Fourier Transform of the signal and integrating over all possible frequencies. This approach gives us the original signal in the time domain. CO - RELATED SUB QUERY " A query written inside another query such that the outer query and the inner query are Dependent on each other , this is known as Co-Related Sub-Query ". WORKING PRINCIPLE : Outer query executes first but partially 1. The partially executed output is given as an input to the inner Query 2. The inner query executes completely and generates an output 3. The output of inner query is fed as an input to the Outer query and Outer 4. Query produces the result . Therefore, we can state that the outer query and the inner query both are INTERDEPENDENT ( dependent on each other ) . 5. Symmetric Key Cryptography Symmetric Key Cryptography is an encryption system where the sender and receiver of a message use a single common key to encrypt and decrypt messages. Symmetric Key cryptography is faster and simpler but the problem is that the sender and receiver have to somehow exchange keys securely. The most popular symmetric key cryptography systems are Data Encryption Systems (DES) and Advanced Encryption Systems (AES) . Symmetric Key Cryptography Symmetric Key Cryptography Example: Data Encryption Standard (DES) DES (Data encryption standard) is an older encryption algorithm that is used to convert 64-bit plaintext data into 48-bit encrypted ciphertext. It uses symmetric keys (which means same key for encryption and decryption). It is kind of old by today’s standard but can be used as a basic building block for learning newer encryption algorithms. Transposition Ciphers: Rearrange the order of characters without changing them. Example: Rail Fence Cipher, where characters are written in a zigzag and read row by row.

Real-Life Use: Basic message encoding to confuse readers. Types of Classical Ciphers There are basic types of Classical Ciphers. Cipher Name Description Real-life/CTF Use Caesar Cipher Each letter is shifted a fixed number of places. Hidden messages in simple malware, games, or emails. Vigenère Cipher Uses a keyword to shift letters; more secure than Caesar. Used in older secret messages and CTF puzzles. Atbash Cipher A → Z, B → Y… Reverses the alphabet. Often seen in basic stego/crypto challenges. ROT13 A Caesar Cipher with a shift of 13. Used in hiding spoilers or light obfuscation online. Rail Fence Cipher A form of transposition cipher that rearranges the order. Great for simple puzzles and password hiding. Steganography Steganography is the practice of concealing information. It involves hiding data within an ordinary, non-secret file or message to prevent detection. The hidden information is being extracted at the receiving end. With the help of Steganography, we can hide any digital content virtually like text, image, videotape, etc. Common Types of Steganography: Here are the types mentioned below about Steganography Image Stego (LSB) Data is hidden in the least significant bits of pixels. Real-Life Use: Malware communication, CTF challenges. Text Stego Secret data hidden using invisible characters, spaces, or misspelled words. Real-Life Use: Covert communication in censored countries. Audio Stego Hidden messages embedded in audio signals, often inaudible. Real-Life Use: Watermarking or espionage. Video Stego Embeds information in video frames or metadata. Real-Life Use: Covert data exfiltration techniques. Metadata Stego Stores data in metadata fields (e.g., EXIF data in images). The UI should rely on deep background tones (e.g., near-blacks and dark grays) accented by subtle, glowing gradients. Structure: Implement a Bento Grid layout. The dashboard must be split into two main sections: ● Sidebar (Left): A slim, collapsible navigation menu. ● Main Content (Right): A dynamic grid containing the following "Bento" tiles: ○ Hero Tile: A large greeting tile ("Welcome back, [Name]") with a daily learning streak indicator. ○ Course Tiles (Dynamic): Smaller tiles displaying active courses fetched from your database. ○ Activity Tile: A medium tile showing a mock contribution graph or activity chart. 2. g active courses fetched from your database. ○ Activity Tile: A medium tile showing a mock contribution graph or activity chart. 2. The Tech Stack & Constraints You must use the following tools. Substitutions are not permitted for this assignment. ● Framework: Next.js (App Router required). ● Database/BaaS: Supabase. ● Styling: Tailwind CSS. ● Animations: Framer Motion (Strict requirement). ● Icons: Lucide React or Radix Icons. Host your code on a public GitHub repository. 2. Deploy the application using Vercel. 3. Include a .env.example file so we know which Supabase environment variables are required. Symmetric Key Cryptography Symmetric Key Cryptography is an encryption system where the sender and receiver of a message use a single common key to encrypt and decrypt messages. Symmetric Key cryptography is faster and simpler but the problem is that the sender and receiver have to somehow exchange keys securely. The most popular symmetric key cryptography systems are Data Encryption Systems (DES) and Advanced Encryption Systems (AES) . Symmetric Key Cryptography Symmetric Key Cryptography Example: Data Encryption Standard (DES) DES (Data encryption standard) is an older encryption algorithm that is used to convert 64-bit plaintext data into 48-bit encrypted ciphertext. It uses symmetric keys (which means same key for encryption and decryption). It is kind of old by today’s standard but can be used as a basic building block for learning newer encryption algorithms. The Inverse Fourier Transform formula is mathematically expressed as: x(t)= 1 2π -∞ ∞ X(ω) e jωt dω Where: x(t) represents the time-domain signal. X(ω) is the Fourier transform of the signal, representing its frequency-domain equivalent. ω is the angular frequency. j is the imaginary unit. I n essence, the Inverse Fourier Transform takes a frequency spectrum, X(ω), and reconstructs the original signal x(t)x(t)x(t) in the time domain.
